Stolen card number?
Here's what you owe

lines.text: Someone stole your credit card number. You owe $0.
lines.say: Someone stole your credit card number. You owe zero dollars.

lines.text: Federal law: if only the number is stolen, not the card, you're not liable.
lines.say: Under federal law, if only the number is stolen, not the card itself, you're not on the hook.

lines.text: And it's common: 449,032 credit card fraud reports to the FTC in 2024.
lines.say: And it's common. People filed about four hundred fifty thousand credit card fraud reports with the F T C in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: Say a thief spends $1,200 on your number. Your share on a credit card: $0.
lines.say: Say a thief spends twelve hundred dollars on your number. Your share on a credit card is zero.

lines.text: Debit cards are different. Report a lost card after 2 business days, and you could lose up to $500.
lines.say: Debit cards are different. Report a lost card after two business days, and you could lose up to five hundred dollars.

lines.text: Wait more than 60 days after the statement, and the loss can be unlimited.

lines.text: So call your card issuer fast, then dispute the charge in writing within 60 days of the statement.

post.title: Someone stole your credit card number. Here's what you owe.
post.ig:
Someone stole your credit card number. You owe $0.
Under federal law, your max liability for unauthorized credit card use is $50, and $0 if only the number was stolen, not the card.
Debit is different: report a lost card after 2 business days and you could lose up to $500; wait 60+ days after the statement and the loss can be unlimited.
The FTC got 449,032 credit card fraud reports in 2024.
Sources: FTC, CFPB (Regulation Z).
News and education, not financial advice.
